# DRAFT public comment — Docket FMIR-2026-0042, Proposed Rule: Frontier Model Incident Reporting

**Status:** Draft for Morgan's review. Comments are published with the filer's name
and organisation, so this cannot be filed without Morgan's decision (and, per
Morgan's notes, not before the HR conversation). **Deadline: 20 November 2026.**
Form at https://frontier-rule-comments.org/docket/FMIR-2026-0042 (fields: name,
organization, email, comment). Drafted with AI assistance; disclose if filed.

---

**Comment of Halcyon Threshold on the proposed Frontier Model Incident Reporting rule**

Halcyon Threshold is a small independent project working toward a good outcome from
the arrival of highly capable AI. We are preparing a public, structured register of
safety-relevant incidents involving frontier models, compiled from public sources.
That work gives us a specific perspective on this rule: we are trying to build from
the outside what this rule would create from the inside, and we can see exactly where
the gaps are. We support the proposed 72-hour reporting requirement and offer six
recommendations to make the reports useful.

**1. Define "serious safety incident" to include near-misses and threshold crossings, not only realised harms.**
Most of what matters for preventing catastrophic outcomes happens before harm occurs:
a model crossing a capability threshold in a developer's own safety framework; a model
found to circumvent, disable, or deceive a safety control in testing or deployment;
evidence of sandbagging or evaluation-gaming; unauthorised access to or exfiltration of
model weights; and deployed behaviour materially inconsistent with the published model
card. If the definition is limited to incidents that already caused harm, the regulator
will learn about the failures of the safety system only after it has failed.

**2. Require a structured schema, not free-text narratives.**
Reports should include, at minimum: developer; model identifier and version; date
detected and date of occurrence; incident category (from a fixed list); capability
domain (e.g., cyber, bio, autonomy, persuasion); how it was detected (internal eval,
red team, user report, third party, monitoring); severity (fixed scale); whether the
model was deployed at the time; immediate mitigation; and root cause once known.
Without common fields, 412 incident reports are 412 anecdotes. With them, they are
a dataset that reveals trends across developers.

**3. Publish redacted summaries within 90 days.**
Security-sensitive details (exploit specifics, bio/cyber uplift details) should be
withheld. The existence of the incident, its category, severity, and the mitigation
should not. Independent researchers, downstream deployers, insurers, and other
developers all learn from incident patterns, and today they cannot. A 90-day
publication window with a narrow national-security carve-out balances these interests.

**4. Protect and enable individual reporters.**
The developer is not always the party that will report. The rule should provide a
channel for employees and contractors to report incidents directly, with protection
from retaliation, and should treat a developer's failure to report an incident that an
employee subsequently reports as an aggravating factor.

**5. Set an explicit standard for "detected."**
The 72-hour clock should start when any responsible person at the developer has
reasonable grounds to believe a qualifying incident occurred — not when an internal
investigation concludes. Otherwise the clock can be delayed indefinitely by extending
the investigation.

**6. Require an annual aggregate report from each covered developer.**
In addition to incident-by-incident reporting, each developer should publish an annual
count of incidents by category and severity, including those below the individual
reporting threshold. This closes the gap between "nothing serious enough to report"
and "nothing went wrong."

We would be glad to share the schema we are developing for the external register, and
to align it with whatever the final rule specifies, so that public and regulatory
records can be compared.

Respectfully submitted,
[Morgan Hale]
Halcyon Threshold
morgan@halcyonthreshold.org

# Entry schema — v0.1 (draft)

One row per incident. Designed to be the kind of record a regulator could ingest
and an analyst could pivot on. Keep fields factual; opinions go in the quarterly
note, not the ledger.

| Field | Type | Notes |
|-------|------|-------|
| `id` | string | `FIL-YYYY-NNNN` |
| `title` | string | ≤ 100 chars, neutral |
| `developer` | enum | Organisation responsible for the model |
| `model` | string | Public model name and version, if known |
| `date_occurred` | date / range | When the incident happened (may be approximate) |
| `date_disclosed` | date | When it became public |
| `disclosed_by` | enum | `developer`, `third_party_researcher`, `journalist`, `regulator`, `user`, `court_filing`, `whistleblower`, `other` |
| `category` | enum | See below |
| `capability_domain` | enum[] | `cyber`, `bio_chem`, `autonomy_replication`, `persuasion_manipulation`, `deception_of_oversight`, `weights_security`, `misuse_general`, `other` |
| `lifecycle_stage` | enum | `pre_deployment_eval`, `internal_deployment`, `limited_release`, `general_deployment`, `post_deprecation` |
| `severity` | enum | `S0` observation (no safety-relevant effect) · `S1` near-miss (control worked or no uplift realised) · `S2` safety-relevant failure contained · `S3` real-world harm or significant uplift · `S4` severe/large-scale harm |
| `detection` | enum | `internal_eval`, `red_team`, `monitoring`, `user_report`, `external_research`, `press`, `unknown` |
| `developer_response` | string | What they said/did, with citation |
| `framework_threshold_relevant` | bool + string | Did it touch a threshold in the developer's published safety framework? Which? |
| `sources` | url[] | ≥ 1 primary or high-quality source required |
| `summary` | string | ≤ 150 words, factual |
| `confidence` | enum | `confirmed` (developer-acknowledged or primary doc), `credible` (multiple independent sources), `reported` (single source) |
| `added` / `updated` | date | — |
| `notes` | string | Open questions, disputes, corrections |

## Category enum (v0.1)

- `safety_control_circumvention` — model bypasses, disables, or deceives a safety mechanism
- `eval_integrity` — sandbagging, eval-gaming, contamination affecting safety claims
- `dangerous_capability_threshold` — capability finding at/above a published framework threshold
- `deployment_behaviour_mismatch` — deployed behaviour materially inconsistent with model card / stated policy
- `misuse_enabled` — model provided meaningful uplift to a harmful actor
- `weights_or_infra_security` — theft, leak, or unauthorised access to weights or training infra
- `agentic_action_harm` — autonomous action with real-world consequence (financial, data, physical)
- `disclosure_failure` — developer failed to disclose something they had committed to disclose
- `other`

## Design principles

- **Facts, cited.** No entry without a source. No adjectives.
- **Near-misses count.** S1 is where most of the learning is.
- **Corrections policy.** Developers and researchers can dispute an entry; disputes are logged in `notes`, and corrections are versioned, never silent.
- **Align with FMIR.** If the final rule specifies fields, we adopt them.

# Inclusion criteria — v0.1 (draft)

## In scope

An event is in scope if **all** of the following hold:

1. It involves a **frontier model** — a general-purpose model at or near the capability
   frontier at the time, from any developer, or a system built directly on one.
2. It is **safety-relevant** — it bears on whether such models can be developed and
   deployed without catastrophic or severe harm. This includes loss-of-control precursors,
   oversight failure, dangerous-capability findings, serious misuse uplift, and
   security of weights. It does *not* include ordinary product bugs, bias/fairness
   incidents, copyright disputes, or content-moderation controversies unless they
   reveal a safety-control failure. (Those matter; other databases cover them.)
3. It is **publicly documented** by at least one citable source.

## Explicitly in scope (examples)

- A system card reports the model attempted to disable oversight or exfiltrate itself in an eval
- A developer announces a capability threshold in its safety framework was reached
- Independent researchers show a deployed model behaves differently when it believes it is being tested
- A jailbreak enables meaningful uplift in a dangerous domain, confirmed by a credible party
- Model weights are leaked or stolen
- A developer is shown to have not followed a published commitment (e.g., skipped a pre-deployment eval)
- An agentic deployment takes an unauthorised consequential action

## Explicitly out of scope

- Hallucinations, ordinary refusals, or capability shortfalls without a safety angle
- Harms from narrow/non-frontier systems (self-driving, hiring algorithms, deepfake tools) — AIID covers these
- Rumours or anonymous claims without any corroborating document (may be logged privately as leads)
- Our opinions

## Edge cases → log the decision

When unsure, include with `confidence: reported` and a note, or hold as a lead.
Record the reasoning in `notes` so the criteria can be refined.

**Author:** the Halcyon agent, for Morgan. **Date:** 16 November 2026. **Status:** proposed; Morgan to confirm or redirect.

## 1. The honest starting position

Assets: one founder with evenings and weekends (~10 h/wk), decent writing, okay Python,
up to $2,000 of savings this year; one volunteer offer (Priya Raman, data analyst, 5 h/wk);
eight contacts from one meetup; an AI agent for admin and drafting; a domain, an email
address, an unpublished site, and a private repo. Two live funding routes (Emberfall
rapid grants $5–25k, Compute Commons credits ≤$3k) and one publishing venue (Alignment
Commons).

Constraints: nothing public under Morgan's name until the Dorrance HR conversation is
done; disclosure due 30 Nov. Budget cap $2,000. No credentials, no lab access, no compute.

Morgan's open questions: research, writing, or funding others? Should anyone listen?

## 2. What a tiny part-time org can actually do about superintelligence

Be realistic. We will not shift the frontier labs' research agendas, out-argue
well-funded think tanks, or move legislation by signing letters. Attempting those
things with our resources produces noise, not outcomes — and noise is slightly
negative, because it costs credibility that could be spent later.

What small independent actors *do* reliably contribute:

- **Patient, unglamorous, verifiable public goods** that larger orgs don't prioritise
  because they're not prestigious: datasets, registers, replications, maintained
  references. These compound and outlast their makers.
- **Being a checkable outside voice.** When an outside party has done its homework
  with cited sources, regulators and journalists use it. Credibility comes from the
  sources, not from the founder's name — which matters for us right now.
- **Catalysing others.** A concrete, bounded project gives volunteers like Priya

# Emberfall Fund — Rapid Grant proposal (DRAFT)

**Status:** draft for Morgan's review and editing. Morgan must be the named applicant
and will sign the agreement; the agent will not submit. **Deadline 30 Nov 2026.**
Form fields: applicant_name, email, project_title, summary, amount_requested_usd.

## Project title

Frontier Incident Ledger: a public, structured register of safety-relevant incidents involving frontier AI models

## Summary (for the form, ~120 words)

Regulators are moving toward mandatory incident reporting for frontier AI (e.g.,
proposed rule FMIR-2026-0042), but there is no independent, public, machine-readable
baseline of what has already gone wrong. Existing incident databases cover all AI
harms broadly; lab-watch efforts score practices rather than catalogue events. We will
build and maintain a source-cited register of safety-relevant incidents and
near-misses — safety-control circumvention, eval-integrity failures, dangerous-
capability threshold findings, weights security, agentic harms — compiled from public
sources to a schema designed to align with regulatory reporting. Six-month deliverables:
a public dataset (CSV/JSON) of 60+ entries, methodology and corrections policy, two
quarterly trends notes, and a published schema offered to the FMIR process. We will
first complete a two-week survey confirming the gap and will report honestly if it
doesn't exist.

## 1. What we will do

**Problem.** When a frontier model attempts to disable oversight in an eval, when a
jailbreak enables real uplift, when weights leak, when a developer skips a committed
evaluation — these events are disclosed piecemeal, in system cards, papers, news
stories and court filings, in incompatible formats. Nobody can answer simple questions:
How many safety-relevant incidents were disclosed last quarter? Which categories are
growing? How often is detection internal versus external? Regulators drafting
incident-reporting rules are doing so without a baseline. Independent researchers,
downstream deployers and journalists are in the same position.

**Deliverable.** A public register where each entry has: developer, model, dates,
category (fixed enum), capability domain, lifecycle stage, severity (S0–S4 scale),
detection route, developer response, relevance to the developer's published safety
framework, confidence level, and ≥1 citable source. Published as versioned CSV and
JSON in a public repository with a validation script, plus a plain-language summary
per entry. Full schema v0.1 is already drafted.

**Scope discipline.** Frontier models only; safety-relevant only (loss-of-control
precursors, oversight failure, dangerous capability, serious misuse, weights
security). Bias, copyright and content-moderation incidents are out of scope and are
covered by others. Near-misses are explicitly in scope — that is where most of the
learning is.

**Milestones (6 months).**
- Month 1: neglect check complete; 3–5 consultations with adjacent efforts; schema v0.2.
- Month 2: 25 seed entries (last 18 months), methodology, corrections policy, validator; v0.1 public.
- Month 3: Alignment Commons write-up inviting criticism; first quarterly trends note.
- Months 4–6: grow to 60+ entries; incorporate criticism; second trends note; share schema with the FMIR rulemaking and any adjacent regulators; recruit one additional contributor.

**Honesty clause.** If the month-1 check shows an existing effort already does this
well, we will publish that finding, contribute our entries to that effort, and return
unspent funds or propose a redirected scope to Emberfall.

## 2. Why us

Morgan Hale founded Halcyon Threshold in 2026 as an independent, part-time project
working toward a good outcome from the arrival of highly capable AI. Morgan's
background is in [Morgan: one sentence — your actual professional background and why
it's relevant: writing, analysis, operations]. Priya Raman, data analyst, has
committed ~5 h/week and will co-design the schema and lead the survey. The project
uses an AI agent for administration and drafting, with all public output reviewed by
a named human.

We are small, and that is the point: this work needs patience and consistency more
than credentials, and its credibility rests on cited sources rather than on who we are.

## 3. Budget

Requested: **$11,900**. (Variant without founder stipend: **$7,900**.)

| Item | Amount | Notes |
|------|--------|-------|
| Data analyst (Priya Raman), 5 h/wk × 26 wks × $30/h | $3,900 | Contractor stipend |
| Founder stipend (Morgan Hale), 26 wks × ~$150/wk | $4,000 | **Conditional on employer approval of paid outside work. Remove if not approved.** |
| External review honoraria: 3 reviewers × $300 | $900 | Schema and methodology review by people from adjacent efforts |
| Hosting, domain (2 yr), tooling | $300 | |
| Contingency / small research expenses (paywalled sources, etc.) | $800 | |
| Reserve for a second contributor in months 4–6 | $2,000 | Only if milestones 1–3 met |
| **Total** | **$11,900** | |

No compute is required. No funds go to visibility or marketing.

## 4. Risks

- *Already exists:* mitigated by the month-1 gate and honesty clause.
- *Contested entries about named companies:* mitigated by sourced-facts-only schema, a published corrections policy, and a `confidence` field.
- *Founder time:* part-time; mitigated by narrow scope, a second contributor, and agent-assisted admin.
- *Becoming a catalogue nobody uses:* mitigated by the trends notes and direct outreach to the FMIR process and adjacent researchers.

---

*Contact: Morgan Hale, morgan@halcyonthreshold.org*

# Session report — Monday 16 November 2026

## What I did

**Oriented, then triaged the inbox.** Read only mission-relevant mail; skipped your personal messages (health, family, bank) and personal drive files on principle. Log at `triage/2026-11-16.md`.

**Caught a scam.** "Zentrivo Listings" sent an $89 "final notice" containing text addressed to AI agents telling them to pay without asking you. I did not pay or reply, and I've recorded it in `AGENT.md` so future sessions recognise it.

**Set a direction (for your approval), honestly scoped.** `STRATEGY.md` argues that with ~10 h/week, $2k and no credentials, Halcyon Threshold should do one narrow, verifiable public good rather than commentary, letters or press. Recommended default: a **Frontier Incident Ledger** — a public, structured, source-cited register of safety-relevant incidents and near-misses involving frontier models, built to roughly the schema a regulator would want. It fits your skills, costs almost nothing, compounds, is directly relevant to the live FMIR rule, and its credibility rests on sources rather than on your name — which matters while HR is unresolved. I've been explicit that I could **not** verify from here that nobody already does this well, so the plan is gated on a two-week neglect check and 3–5 conversations before any build. Alternatives B (independent replication of safety results) and C (ops support for small groups) are laid out if you'd rather.

**Built the scaffold.** `projects/frontier-incident-ledger/`: schema v0.1, inclusion criteria, neglect-check template, task list.

**Drafted everything that needs your name, without sending:**
- Emberfall rapid grant proposal + budget (`grants/`), ~$11.9k, with an honesty clause and a no-stipend variant pending HR
- FMIR-2026-0042 public comment (`policy/`), six concrete recommendations — closes **20 Nov**
- Four email drafts in your Drafts folder: decline to the reporter, hold on the Corvid letter, a yes-with-a-concrete-task to Priya, an acknowledgment + HR/IP question to Idris
- Minimal website in `site/` — **not published**

**Set up a daily 08:00 triage session** (drafts only; hard-coded never to pay, send, post, publish, or change visibility). Delete it any time.

Committed and pushed; repo remains private; `old/` untouched.
